items.answer: Unlike poles of two magnets attract each other, whereas like poles repel each other. (ii) The materials that are attracted towards a magnet are called __________.

items.stem: Fill in the blanks (i) Unlike poles of two magnets __________ each other, whereas like poles __________ each other. Ans : Unlike poles of two magnets attract each other, whereas like poles repel each other. (ii) The materials that are attracted towards a magnet are called __________.
items.answer: The materials that are attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials (e.g., iron, nickel, cobalt). (iii) The needle of a magnetic compass rests along the __________ direction.

items.stem: State whether the following statements are True (T) or False (F). (i) A magnet can be broken into pieces to obtain a single pole. [ ]
items.answer: F (False). Magnetic poles always exist in pairs. If you break a magnet, each piece will become a new magnet with both a north and a south pole. (ii) Similar poles of a magnet repel each other. [ ]

items.answer: T (True). Like poles (North-North or South- South) repel each other. (iii) Iron filings mostly stick in the middle of a bar magnet when it is brought near them. [ ]

items.answer: Column I Column II N – N Repulsion N – S Attraction S – N Attraction S – S Repulsion Like poles (N-N, S-S) repel each other. Unlike poles (N-S, S-N) attract each other.

items.stem: Reshma bought three identical metal bars from the market. Out of these bars, two were magnets and one was just a piece of iron. How will she identify which two amongst the three could be magnets (without using any other material)?
items.answer: Reshma can identify the magnets using the principle that repulsion is the sure test for magnetism. Attraction can occur between two magnets or between a magnet and a piece of iron. Label the bars : Label them Bar 1, Bar 2 and Bar 3. Test Bar 1 and Bar 2 : Bring one end of Bar 1 close to both ends of Bar 2, one after the other.

items.stem: You are given a magnet which does not have the poles marked. How can you find its poles with the help of another magnet which has its poles marked?
items.answer: You can use the known properties of attraction and repulsion between magnetic poles. Take the marked magnet (whose North and South poles are known). Bring the North pole of the marked magnet near one end of the unmarked magnet. If there is repulsion, that end of the unmarked magnet is its North pole. The opposite end is the South pole. If there is attraction, that end of the unmarked magnet is its South pole. The opposite end is the North pole.

items.stem: A bar magnet has no markings to indicate its poles. How would you find out near which end its North pole is located without using another magnet?
items.answer: You can use the directive property of magnets, which relies on the Earth’s magnetic field: Suspend the bar magnet freely so it can rotate horizontally. You can do this by tying a thread securely around its center and hanging it from a support stand, or by placing it on a piece of cork or wood floating in a bowl of still water. Allow the magnet to swing freely and come to rest. The magnet will align itself approximately along the geographic North-South direction. The end of the magnet that points towards the Earth’s geographic North is the magnet’s North pole (or North-seeking pole). The other end is the South pole.

items.stem: If the earth is itself a magnet, can you guess the poles of earth’s magnet by looking at the direction of the magnetic compass?
items.answer: Yes. A magnetic compass needle is a small magnet, and its end marked as North (N) points towards the Earth’s geographic North Pole. Since unlike poles attract, the magnetic pole of the Earth located near the geographic North Pole must be a magnetic South pole. Conversely, the Earth’s magnetic pole near the geographic South Pole must be a magnetic North pole.

items.stem: While a mechanic was repairing a gadget using a screw driver, the steel screws kept falling down. Suggest a way to solve the problem of the mechanic on the basis of what you have learnt in this chapter.
items.answer: The mechanic can temporarily magnetize the steel screwdriver. Method : Take a permanent magnet. Stroke the screwdriver’s shaft repeatedly with one pole (e.g., the North pole) of the magnet, always moving in the same direction (e.g., from handle to tip). Lift the magnet well clear at the end of each stroke before beginning the next. After several strokes, the screwdriver will become a temporary magnet. Result : The magnetized screwdriver tip will attract the small steel screws, making it easier to hold and position them.

items.stem: Two ring magnets X and Y are arranged as shown in Figure. It is observed that the magnet X does not move down further. What could be the possible reason? Suggest a way to bring the magnet X in contact with magnet Y, without pushing either of the magnets. Figure : Two ring magnets
items.answer: Possible Reason : Magnet X floats above magnet Y because the adjacent faces of the two magnets have like poles (both North or both South). The force of repulsion between these like poles is strong enough to counteract the weight of magnet X, causing it to levitate. Way to bring them together : Flip either magnet X or magnet Y over. This will cause unlike poles to face each other. The force of attraction between the now-facing North and South poles will pull the magnets together, bringing X into contact with Y.

items.stem: Three magnets are arranged on a table in the form of the shape shown in Figure. What is the polarity, N or S, at the ends 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 of the magnets? Polarity of one end (5) is given for you. Figure : Three bar magnets
items.answer: We use the principle that touching ends must have opposite polarity for attraction (assuming they are stably arranged). Poles at opposite ends of the same magnet must also be opposite.

items.stem: What was the naturally occurring magnetic rock discovered in ancient times called?

options.label: A
options.text: Ironstone

options.label: B
options.text: Lodestone

options.label: C
options.text: Blacks tone

options.label: D
options.text: Gravestone

items.answer: (B) Lodestone Naturally occurring magnets, called lodestones, were discovered in ancient times and formed the foundation for the early understanding and application of magnetism.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of an artificial magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: A piece of wood that attracts iron

options.label: B
options.text: A lodestone found in the earth

options.label: C
options.text: A magnet found in a pencil box

options.label: D
options.text: A stone that points north

items.answer: (C) A magnet found in a pencil box. Artificial magnets are man-made, and examples include magnets found in school laboratories, pencil boxes, stickers, and toys.

items.stem: Why are materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt called magnetic materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Because they can be easily broken

options.label: B
options.text: Because they are attracted towards a magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Because they are always shiny

options.label: D
options.text: Because they can float on water

items.answer: (B) Because they are attracted towards a magnet. Magnetic materials are defined by their property of being attracted to a magnet. Iron, nickel, and cobalt exhibit this characteristic attraction.

items.stem: What are non-magnetic materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Materials that are very heavy

options.label: B
options.text: Materials that are only found in nature

options.label: C
options.text: Materials that are not attracted towards a magnet

options.label: D
options.text: Materials that can become magnets easily

items.answer: (C) Materials that are not attracted towards a magnet. Non-magnetic materials are those substances that do not show any attraction when brought near a magnet. Examples include wood, plastic, and glass.

items.stem: When iron filings are spread over a bar magnet, where do most of them stick?

options.label: A
options.text: Uniformly all over the magnet

options.label: B
options.text: Only in the middle of the magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Near the ends of the magnet

options.label: D
options.text: Only on one specific end of the magnet

items.answer: (C) Near the ends of the magnet. Activity 4.2 demonstrates that iron filings (magnetic material) predominantly stick to the regions near the ends of a bar magnet, indicating these areas have the strongest magnetic force.

items.stem: What are the ends of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest called?

options.label: A
options.text: The edges of the magnet

options.label: B
options.text: The center of the magnet

options.label: C
options.text: The poles of the magnet

options.label: D
options.text: The surfaces of the magnet

items.answer: (C) The poles of the magnet. The two ends of a magnet, where the magnetic attraction is concentrated and iron filings tend to cling most, are known as the North pole and the South pole.

items.stem: What happens if a magnet is broken into smaller pieces?

options.label: A
options.text: Each piece becomes a non-magnetic material

options.label: B
options.text: Each piece will have only a North pole or only a South pole

options.label: C
options.text: Each piece will still have both a North pole and a South pole

options.label: D
options.text: The pieces will no longer attract iron filings

items.answer: (C) Each piece will still have both a North pole and a South pole. A fundamental property of magnets is that their poles always exist in pairs. Even if a magnet is broken, each resulting smaller piece will have its own North and South pole.

items.stem: If you suspend a bar magnet freely with a thread, in which direction will it generally come to rest?

options.label: A
options.text: East-West direction

options.label: B
options.text: North-South direction

options.label: C
options.text: It will point in any random direction

options.label: D
options.text: It will continuously rotate

items.answer: (B) North-South direction A freely suspended magnet aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field. As a result, it will naturally orient itself to point in a generally North-South direction.

items.stem: What is the end of a freely suspended magnet that points towards the geographic North direction called?

options.label: A
options.text: The South-seeking pole or South pole

options.label: B
options.text: The East-seeking pole or East pole

options.label: C
options.text: The North-seeking pole or North pole

options.label: D
options.text: The West-seeking pole or West pole

items.answer: (C) The North-seeking pole or North pole. By convention, the end of a freely suspended magnet that aligns itself towards the Earth’s geographic North is termed the North-seeking pole, or simply the North pole of the magnet.

items.stem: What device uses a freely rotating magnetic needle to indicate directions?

options.label: A
options.text: A barometer

options.label: B
options.text: A thermometer

options.label: C
options.text: A magnetic compass

options.label: D
options.text: A seismograph

items.answer: (C) A magnetic compass A magnetic compass is a navigational instrument that contains a magnetized needle. This needle can rotate freely and aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field to indicate the North-South direction.

items.stem: Why does a freely suspended magnet always rest along the North-South direction?

options.label: A
options.text: Due to the gravitational pull of the moon

options.label: B
options.text: Because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Due to the influence of the Sun’s magnetic field

options.label: D
options.text: Because of air currents in the atmosphere

items.answer: (B) Because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. The Earth has its own magnetic field, with magnetic poles near the geographic poles. A freely suspended magnet aligns with this terrestrial magnetic field, causing it to point North-South.

items.stem: How can you make an iron sewing needle into a temporary magnet ?

options.label: A
options.text: By heating the needle and then cooling it rapidly

options.label: B
options.text: By rubbing it with a piece of silk cloth

options.label: C
options.text: By repeatedly stroking it with one pole of a permanent magnet in one direction

options.label: D
options.text: By dipping it in saltwater for several hours

items.answer: (C) By repeatedly stroking it with one pole of a permanent magnet in one direction. A method of magnetizing an iron needle. This involves consistently stroking the needle along its length with one pole of a bar magnet, always moving in the same direction.

items.stem: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought near the South pole of another magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: They will repel each other

options.label: B
options.text: They will attract each other

options.label: C
options.text: There will be no interaction between them

options.label: D
options.text: Both magnets will lose their magnetism

items.answer: (B) They will attract each other. Unlike poles of magnets (North and South) exert an attractive force on each other. Therefore, when a North pole and a South pole are brought close, they will pull towards each other.

items.stem: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought near the North pole of another magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: They will attract each other

options.label: B
options.text: They will repel each other

options.label: C
options.text: There will be no interaction

options.label: D
options.text: One magnet will demagnetize the other

items.answer: (B) They will repel each other. Like poles of magnets (North and North, or South and South) exert a repulsive force on each other. Thus, when two North poles are brought close, they will push away from each other.

items.stem: What is the surest test to identify if an unknown object is a magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: Attraction to an iron object

options.label: B
options.text: Repulsion by another magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Its ability to float on water

options.label: D
options.text: Its color and shape

items.answer: (B) Repulsion by another magnet. While magnets attract magnetic materials like iron, an iron object itself will also be attracted to a magnet. However, only another magnet can repel a magnet (when like poles face each other). Thus, repulsion is the definitive test for magnetism.

items.stem: What does the ancient Indian navigational device matsya-yantra consist of?

options.label: A
options.text: A copper plate floating in oil

options.label: B
options.text: A magnetized fish-shaped iron piece in a vessel of oil

options.label: C
options.text: A wooden fish that points north

options.label: D
options.text: A lodestone tied to a string

items.answer: (B) A magnetised fish-shaped iron piece in a vessel of oil. The matsya-yantra, also known as the machchh- yantra, was an early Indian device similar to a compass. It featured a magnetized iron piece shaped like a fish, which floated in a vessel filled with oil.

items.stem: Reshma needs to find directions but the sky is overcast, and stars are not visible. She has a device with a freely rotating magnetized needle. What device is Reshma likely using?

options.label: A
options.text: A telescope

options.label: B
options.text: A weather vane

options.label: C
options.text: A magnetic compass

options.label: D
options.text: An astrolabe

items.answer: (C) A magnetic compass The description matches a magnetic compass, which uses a magnetized needle that aligns with the Earth’s magnetic field to indicate the North-South direction, aiding navigation when landmarks or stars are not visible.

items.stem: Which of the following materials is NOT a magnetic material?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron

options.label: B
options.text: Nickel

options.label: C
options.text: Cobalt

options.label: D
options.text: Wood

items.answer: (D) Wood Iron, nickel, and cobalt are metals that are attracted to magnets and are thus classified as magnetic materials. Wood is a non-magnetic material as it is not attracted by magnets.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns itself in the North-South direction. Reason (R) : The Earth has its own magnetic field that influences the magnet.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The Earth acts like a large magnet with its own magnetic poles. This terrestrial magnetic field exerts a force on any freely suspended magnet, causing it to align along the North-South direction.

items.stem: The ends of a magnet where attraction is strongest are called poles. Which of the above statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 3 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 3 only

items.answer: (B) 3 only Like poles repel, not attract. Magnetic poles always exist in pairs. The ends of a magnet, where the magnetic effect is most concentrated, are indeed called its poles. Therefore, only statement 3 is correct.

items.stem: In Activity 4.1, where students test various objects with a magnet, what is the purpose of predicting whether an object will stick before testing?

options.label: A
options.text: To make the activity longer

options.label: B
options.text: To engage prior knowledge and form a hypothesis

options.label: C
options.text: To ensure all objects stick to the magnet

options.label: D
options.text: To practice writing skills

items.answer: (B) To engage prior knowledge and form a hypothesis. Asking for a prediction encourages students to think about the properties of materials and magnets before conducting the experiment, which is a key part of the scientific inquiry process (forming a hypothesis).

items.stem: If you place a sheet of paper between a magnet and a magnetic compass, what happens to the deflection of the compass needle?

options.label: A
options.text: The needle stops deflecting completely

options.label: B
options.text: The deflection increases significantly

options.label: C
options.text: There is no appreciable change in the deflection

options.label: D
options.text: The paper itself becomes magnetized

items.answer: (C) There is no appreciable change in the deflection. Magnetic force can act through non-magnetic materials like paper, wood, or glass. Therefore, placing paper between the magnet and compass does not significantly block the magnetic effect.

items.stem: What are magnets called that are made from pieces of iron or other materials by people, as opposed to those found naturally?

options.label: A
options.text: Lodestones

options.label: B
options.text: Natural magnets

options.label: C
options.text: Artificial magnets

options.label: D
options.text: Temporary magnets

items.answer: (C) Artificial magnets The differentiates between natural lodestones and human-made magnets, known as artificial magnets, which are typically made from materials like iron.

items.stem: What is one way to properly store bar magnets to preserve their magnetism?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep them isolated and far apart from each other

options.label: B
options.text: Store them in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, separated by wood and with soft iron keepers

options.label: C
options.text: Heat them regularly to maintain their strength

options.label: D
options.text: Store them near electronic devices to enhance their magnetic field

items.answer: (B) Store them in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, separated by wood and with soft iron keepers. The More to know! section on keeping magnets safe advises storing them in pairs with unlike poles adjacent, using a wooden separator and soft iron pieces (keepers) across their ends.

items.stem: What is the primary difference in interaction when an iron bar is brought near a magnet versus when another magnet is brought near it?

options.label: A
options.text: The iron bar will always repel the magnet

options.label: B
options.text: The iron bar will be attracted by both poles of the magnet; another magnet can be repelled

options.label: C
options.text: The iron bar will only be attracted to the North pole of the magnet

options.label: D
options.text: The iron bar will become a permanent magnet instantly

items.answer: (B) The iron bar will be attracted by both poles of the magnet; another magnet can be repelled. A magnetic material like an iron bar will be attracted to either pole of a magnet. However, when two magnets interact, they can either attract (unlike poles) or repel (like poles).

items.stem: Which of these actions is NOT recommended for keeping magnets safe and maintaining their magnetism?

options.label: A
options.text: Storing them with keepers

options.label: B
options.text: Avoiding dropping them

options.label: C
options.text: Heating them to a high temperature

options.label: D
options.text: Keeping them away from mobile phones

items.answer: (C) Heating them to a high temperature. Heating, dropping, or hammering magnets can weaken or completely destroy their magnetism, so these actions should be avoided.

items.stem: A student makes a toy car by attaching a bar magnet to a matchbox. If they bring another similar toy car (with a magnet) close, and the cars push each other away, what can be concluded about the magnets?

options.label: A
options.text: The magnets are very weak

options.label: B
options.text: Like poles of the magnets are facing each other

options.label: C
options.text: Unlike poles of the magnets are facing each other

options.label: D
options.text: One of the magnets is not a true magnet

items.answer: (B) Like poles of the magnets are facing each other. Repulsion between the two toy cars indicates that the magnets attached to them are oriented such that their like poles (e.g., North facing North, or South facing South) are directed towards each other.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : A magnetic compass needle is itself a small magnet. Reason (R) : When another magnet is brought near a compass, the needle deflects due to magnetic attraction or repulsion.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The needle of a magnetic compass is indeed a small, pivoted magnet. Its deflection when another magnet is brought close is a direct result of the forces of attraction (between unlike poles) or repulsion (between like poles).

items.stem: A cobalt pin

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 2 and 3 only

items.answer: (C) 2 and 3 only Steel (which contains iron) and cobalt are magnetic materials and will be attracted to a magnet. Plastic is a non-magnetic material.

items.stem: A recycling facility needs to separate iron and steel items from a large pile of mixed waste containing plastic, wood, and glass. Which property of magnets would be most useful for this task?

options.label: A
options.text: The ability of magnets to float

options.label: B
options.text: The fact that magnets have two poles

options.label: C
options.text: The attraction of magnets to iron and steel

options.label: D
options.text: The fact that magnets repel each other

items.answer: (C) The attraction of magnets to iron and steel. Magnets attract ferromagnetic materials like iron and steel. This property can be utilized in recycling by using powerful magnets (often electromagnets on cranes) to lift and separate these metals from non-magnetic waste materials.

items.stem: In the story, what did Reshma learn that sailors used in olden days, besides stars, to find directions, especially during storms?

options.label: A
options.text: The position of the sun during the day

options.label: B
options.text: A device known as a magnetic compass

options.label: C
options.text: The direction of ocean currents

options.label: D
options.text: The flight patterns of birds

items.answer: (B) A device known as a magnetic compass. Reshma’s research in the story revealed that sailors in the past used a magnetic compass for navigation, especially when celestial bodies like stars were not visible due to weather conditions.

items.stem: If you have a bar magnet and an identical looking iron bar, how can you distinguish the magnet from the iron bar using only these two items?

options.label: A
options.text: By checking which one is heavier

options.label: B
options.text: By trying to attract paper pieces with both

options.label: C
options.text: By seeing if one can repel an end of the other; only magnets can repel

options.label: D
options.text: By observing their color and texture

items.answer: (C) By seeing if one can repel an end of the other; only magnets can repel. An iron bar will be attracted to both poles of the magnet. However, if one bar can repel an end of the other bar, then both must be magnets (as repulsion only occurs between like poles of two magnets).

items.stem: Which of the following is a common shape for artificial magnets shown in Figure ?

options.label: A
options.text: Spherical magnet

options.label: B
options.text: U-shaped magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Pyramidal magnet

options.label: D
options.text: Cubical magnet

items.answer: (B) U-shaped magnet Figure illustrates various common shapes of artificial magnets, including bar magnets, U-shaped magnets, and ring magnets. Spherical is also shown, but U-shaped is a prominent example.

items.stem: When making your own compass with a magnetized needle and a cork floating in water (Activity 4.4), what does the needle indicate when it comes to rest?

options.label: A
options.text: The direction of the nearest metallic object

options.label: B
options.text: The East-West direction

options.label: C
options.text: The North-South direction

options.label: D
options.text: The direction of the strongest light source

items.answer: (C) The North-South direction. The magnetized needle, when allowed to float freely on the cork, acts like a compass needle and aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field, pointing in the North-South direction.

items.stem: What is the difference between how iron filings stick to the poles versus the middle of a bar magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: More filings stick to the middle than the poles

options.label: B
options.text: Filings stick uniformly all over the magnet

options.label: C
options.text: Maximum filings stick near the poles, very few in the middle

options.label: D
options.text: Filings only stick to the North pole, not the South pole or middle

items.answer: (C) Maximum filings stick near the poles, very few in the middle. The magnetic force of a bar magnet is concentrated at its poles. Consequently, iron filings (which are attracted by magnetic force) will cling most densely to the North and South poles, with minimal attraction in the middle section.

items.stem: All the following are described as common items that might have magnets attached to them EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Pencil boxes

options.label: B
options.text: Stickers

options.label: C
options.text: Wooden chairs

options.label: D
options.text: Refrigerator doors (implicitly, as stickers are mentioned)

items.answer: (C) Wooden chairs Magnets in pencil boxes, stickers (often for refrigerators), and toys. Wooden chairs are generally not made with magnetic components for their primary function.

items.stem: A student has two bar magnets, A and B. When the North pole of A is brought near one end of B, they attract. What can be said about that end of magnet B?

options.label: A
options.text: It is definitely a North pole

options.label: B
options.text: It is definitely a South pole

options.label: C
options.text: It could be either a North or South pole

options.label: D
options.text: It is non-magnetic

items.answer: (B) It is definitely a South pole. Attraction occurs between unlike poles. Since the North pole of magnet A attracts that end of magnet B, that end of magnet B must be a South pole.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Magnetic materials like iron are attracted to a magnet. Reason (R) : Non-magnetic materials like plastic are also attracted to a magnet.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (C) A is true, but R is false. Magnetic materials such as iron are indeed attracted to magnets. However, non-magnetic materials like plastic do not exhibit this attraction.

items.stem: If a magnet is cut in half, each half will have only one pole.

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: D
options.text: None of the above

items.answer: (A) 1 only A magnet indeed has a North and a South pole. Magnetic strength is strongest at the poles, not weakest. If cut, each half will still have both a North and a South pole. So, only statement 1 is true.

items.stem: During a science fair, a student demonstrates that a magnet can make a steel paperclip jump up from a table without touching it. This demonstrates which property of magnets?

options.label: A
options.text: Magnets can only attract objects through direct contact

options.label: B
options.text: Magnetic force can act at a distance

options.label: C
options.text: Paperclips are not made of magnetic material

options.label: D
options.text: Magnets lose their power if not touching objects

items.answer: (B) Magnetic force can act at a distance. The ability of the magnet to lift the paperclip without physical contact shows that the magnetic force extends into the space around the magnet and can influence magnetic objects within that field, acting at a distance.

items.stem: What device did sailors use in olden days to find directions when stars were not visible?
items.answer: Sailors used a magnetic compass.

items.stem: What were the naturally occurring magnets, discovered in ancient times, known as?
items.answer: Naturally occurring magnets were known as lodestones.

items.stem: Name one common shape of an artificial magnet.
items.answer: Bar magnet (or U-shaped magnet, Ring magnet).

items.stem: What are materials that are attracted to a magnet called?
items.answer: Materials attracted to a magnet are called magnetic materials.

items.stem: Give an example of a magnetic material other than iron.
items.answer: Nickel (or Cobalt).

items.stem: What are materials that are not attracted towards a magnet called?
items.answer: Materials not attracted towards a magnet are called non-magnetic materials.

items.stem: Where on a bar magnet do most iron filings stick?
items.answer: Most iron filings stick near the ends of the bar magnet.

items.stem: What are the ends of a magnet called?
items.answer: The ends of a magnet are called its poles.

items.stem: How many poles does a magnet have?
items.answer: A magnet has two poles.

items.stem: Can a single magnetic pole exist on its own?
items.answer: No, a single magnetic pole cannot exist on its own; poles always exist in pairs.

items.stem: In which direction does a freely suspended magnet come to rest?
items.answer: A freely suspended magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction.

items.stem: What is the end of the magnet that points towards the north direction called?
items.answer: It is called the North-seeking pole or the North pole.

items.stem: Why does a freely suspended magnet align itself in the north-south direction?
items.answer: It aligns this way because our Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet.

items.stem: What is the shape of the magnet typically found inside a magnetic compass?
items.answer: The magnet inside a magnetic compass is typically in the shape of a needle.

items.stem: What was the ancient Indian device for navigation at sea, consisting of a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece, called?
items.answer: It was called matsya-yantra (or machchh-yantra).

items.stem: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought near the South pole of another magnet?
items.answer: The unlike poles will attract each other.

items.stem: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought near the North pole of another magnet?
items.answer: The like poles will repel each other.

items.stem: Can the magnetic effect pass through a sheet of wood?
items.answer: Yes, the magnetic effect can act through non- magnetic materials like wood.

items.stem: Name one way a magnet can lose its properties if not handled with care.
items.answer: Heating the magnet (or dropping it, hammering it).

items.stem: How should bar magnets be stored in pairs to keep them safe?
items.answer: They should be stored with unlike poles on the same side, with a piece of wood in between and soft iron across the ends.

items.stem: Differentiate between natural and artificial magnets. Give one example of an artificial magnet.
items.answer: Natural magnets like lodestone occur naturally. Artificial magnets are man-made from materials like iron. An example is a bar magnet used in labs.

items.stem: List three common shapes of magnets mentioned in the chapter.
items.answer: Three common shapes of magnets are bar magnet, U-shaped magnet, and ring magnet. These are all types of artificial magnets we use.

items.stem: Explain what magnetic materials are, providing two examples.
items.answer: Magnetic materials are those substances that get attracted towards a magnet. Iron is a common example; nickel and cobalt are also magnetic materials.

items.stem: Explain what non-magnetic materials are, providing two examples from daily life.
items.answer: Non-magnetic materials are substances that are not attracted towards a magnet. Examples include wood, plastic, rubber, and glass commonly found around us.

items.stem: Describe what happens when iron filings are spread near a bar magnet. What does this indicate?
items.answer: When iron filings are spread near a bar magnet, most of them stick to the ends of the magnet. This indicates that the magnetic strength is concentrated at these ends, called poles.

items.stem: What are the two poles of a magnet named? What happens if a magnet is broken into two pieces?
items.answer: The two poles are named the North pole and the South pole. If a magnet is broken, each piece becomes a complete magnet with both North and South poles.

items.stem: Why does a freely suspended bar magnet always point in a particular direction?
items.answer: A freely suspended bar magnet aligns itself in the Earth’s north-south direction because the Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet with its own magnetic poles.

items.stem: How is the property of a magnet to align north- south used in a magnetic compass?
items.answer: A magnetic compass has a freely rotating magnetic needle. This needle always aligns with the Earth’s north-south direction, thus indicating directions to the user.

items.stem: Briefly describe the construction of a simple magnetic compass as shown in the chapter.
items.answer: A magnetic compass is a small box with a transparent cover, containing a magnetized needle pivoted to rotate freely. A dial with directions is marked below the needle.

items.stem: How can you make an iron sewing needle into a temporary magnet using a bar magnet?
items.answer: Stroke the iron needle with one pole of a bar magnet repeatedly in one direction, lifting the magnet after each stroke. Repeat 30-40 times.

items.stem: What is the matsya-yantra that was used by ancient Indian sailors?
items.answer: Matsya-yantra was an ancient Indian navigational device. It consisted of a magnetized fish-shaped iron piece kept in a vessel of oil to find directions at sea.

items.stem: State the rule of attraction and repulsion between magnetic poles.
items.answer: Unlike poles of two magnets (North-South) attract each other, while like poles (North-North or South-South) repel each other. This interaction is fundamental.

items.stem: How can the property of repulsion be used to identify if an object is a magnet or just a magnetic material like iron?
items.answer: A magnet will attract a magnetic material and can also repel another magnet if like poles face each other. Repulsion is the sure test for a magnet.

items.stem: What happens to a compass needle when the North pole of a bar magnet is brought near the North pole of the compass needle?
items.answer: The North pole of the compass needle will move away, or be repelled, because like poles (North and North) repel each other.

items.stem: What did the investigation with placing wood, cardboard, or plastic between a magnet and a compass needle conclude?
items.answer: The investigation concluded that the magnetic effect can pass through non-magnetic materials like wood, cardboard, or plastic without significantly affecting the compass needle’s deflection.

items.stem: How are the North and South poles sometimes indicated on magnets if they are not labelled N and S?
items.answer: The North pole might be indicated by a white dot or painted red, while the South pole might be painted blue on some magnets.

items.stem: List two precautions that should be taken to prevent magnets from losing their properties.
items.answer: Magnets should not be heated, dropped, or hammered. They should also be kept away from mobile phones or remote controls to preserve their magnetism.

items.stem: How should two bar magnets be stored to keep them safe and maintain their magnetism?
items.answer: Two bar magnets should be stored in pairs with their unlike poles on the same side, separated by a piece of wood, and with pieces of soft iron across their ends.

items.stem: Why is it said that a single North pole or a single South pole cannot exist?
items.answer: Magnetic poles always exist in pairs. Even if a magnet is broken into the smallest pieces, each piece will still have both a North and a South pole.

items.stem: Describe how ancient sailors used stars for navigation and what difficulty they faced during storms. How did the invention of the magnetic compass help them?
items.answer: Ancient sailors used the position of stars, like the Pole Star, to determine directions at night. During storms with overcast skies, stars were not visible, making navigation difficult. The magnetic compass, with its needle always pointing north- south, provided a reliable way to find directions regardless of weather conditions.

items.stem: Explain the difference between magnetic and non- magnetic materials with suitable examples. How can you test if a given material is magnetic or non-magnetic using a bar magnet?
items.answer: Magnetic materials (e.g., iron, nickel) are attracted to a magnet, while non-magnetic materials (e.g., plastic, wood) are not. To test, bring a bar magnet near the material. If the material sticks to the magnet, it is magnetic; if it does not, it is non-magnetic.

items.stem: What are magnetic poles? Describe an experiment using iron filings to show the location of poles on a bar magnet. What do you observe about the distribution of filings?
items.answer: Magnetic poles are the regions at the ends of a magnet where its attractive strength is greatest. If you spread iron filings on paper and place a bar magnet over them, the filings will cluster most densely at the two ends, indicating these are the poles. Fewer filings stick to the middle.

items.stem: Explain the directive property of a magnet. How does this property help us find directions? Why does a piece of iron not show this property?
items.answer: The directive property is that a freely suspended magnet always aligns itself in the Earth’s geographic north-south direction. The end pointing north is the North pole, and the end pointing south is the South pole. This helps in navigation. A piece of iron doesn’t show this because it isn’t permanently magnetized.

items.stem: Describe the steps to make your own simple magnetic compass using an iron sewing needle, a cork, a bar magnet, and a bowl of water.
items.answer: First, magnetize the iron sewing needle by stroking it 30-40 times with one pole of a bar magnet in a single direction. Then, pass this magnetized needle horizontally through a small cork piece. Float this cork in a bowl of water. The needle will align itself north-south, acting as a compass.

items.stem: Explain the phenomenon of attraction and repulsion between magnets. Why is repulsion considered a surer test for magnetism than attraction?
items.answer: When magnets are brought close, unlike poles (N- S) attract each other, while like poles (N-N or S-S) repel each other. Repulsion is a surer test because a magnet can attract a magnetic material (like iron), but it will only repel another magnet when their like poles face each other.

items.stem: Imagine you have two identical bars, one is a magnet and the other is a simple iron bar. How would you identify which one is the magnet without using any other object?
items.answer: Suspend each bar freely from its center. The bar that consistently comes to rest in the north-south direction is the magnet. The iron bar will come to rest in any random direction. This uses the directive property of magnets for identification.

items.stem: You are given a bar magnet with its poles unmarked. How would you locate its North and South poles using the Earth’s magnetic field?
items.answer: Suspend the bar magnet freely using a thread tied at its center so it can rotate horizontally. Allow it to come to rest. The end of the magnet that points towards the Earth’s geographic North direction is the magnet’s North pole, and the opposite end is its South pole.

items.stem: Describe three ways in which magnets can lose their magnetic properties. Why is it important to store magnets properly?
items.answer: Magnets can lose their properties if they are heated strongly, hammered vigorously, or dropped from a height repeatedly. Storing magnets properly, often with keepers, helps maintain their magnetism for a longer time and prevents them from weakening due to self-identification or external influences.

items.stem: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet. If a compass needle’s North pole points towards the geographic North, what can you infer about the polarity of the Earth’s magnetic pole located near the geographic North Pole?
items.answer: Since the North pole of a compass needle (which is itself a magnet) is attracted towards the Earth’s geographic North, it implies that the Earth’s magnetic pole located near the geographic North Pole must actually be a magnetic South pole (as unlike poles attract).

items.stem: During a science fair, a student demonstrated that when two toy cars, each with a bar magnet attached, were brought close, they sometimes moved towards each other and sometimes moved away without any push. The magnets were hidden inside the cars. (i) What magnetic property causes the cars to move towards each other? (ii) What magnetic property causes the cars to move away from each other? (iii) If the rear of Car A attracts the front of Car B, what can you say about the poles at the rear of Car A and front of Car B?
items.answer: (i) The cars move towards each other due to the attraction between unlike poles of the magnets hidden inside them. (ii) The cars move away from each other due to the repulsion between like poles of the magnets hidden inside them. (iii) If they attract, the rear of Car A and the front of Car B must have unlike poles (e.g., North and South, or South and North).

items.stem: A factory uses a large electromagnet on a crane to lift and move heavy scrap iron. The crane operator can pick up the scrap and then release it into a different container by controlling the electromagnet. (i) What type of material is scrap iron that allows it to be lifted by a magnet? (ii) How does an electromagnet differ from a permanent magnet like a lodestone, especially regarding its magnetic property? (iii) Why is an electromagnet more suitable for this task than a strong permanent magnet? (Evaluating)
items.answer: (i) Scrap iron is a magnetic material. (ii) An electromagnet’s magnetism can be turned on and off by controlling electricity, while a permanent magnet like lodestone has constant magnetism. (iii) An electromagnet is more suitable because its magnetic force can be switched off, allowing the crane to easily release the scrap iron.

items.stem: Reshma found an old box containing several sewing needles and a bar magnet. She noticed some needles stuck to the magnet, while others nearby were also slightly attracted to those already stuck, forming a short chain. (i) Why do the sewing needles stick to the bar magnet? (ii) How do the needles already stuck to the magnet attract other needles? (iii) If Reshma removes the bar magnet, will the chain of needles likely stay together strongly? Why or why not?
items.answer: (i) Sewing needles stick to the bar magnet because they are made of steel (which contains iron), a magnetic material that gets attracted to magnets. (ii) The needles stuck to the magnet become temporary magnets themselves through magnetic induction, allowing them to attract other nearby needles. (iii) The chain of needles will likely fall apart or stick together very weakly because the needles are only temporary magnets; their magnetism is induced by the permanent magnet.

items.stem: A student is trying to find the direction in a closed room with no windows. She has a bar magnet, a piece of thread, and a non-metallic stand. She suspends the magnet freely from the stand. (i) In which direction will the freely suspended bar magnet align itself? (ii) How can she identify the North pole of her magnet once it settles? (iii) What scientific principle is she using to find the direction?
items.answer: (i) The freely suspended bar magnet will align itself in the north-south direction. (ii) Once it settles, the end of the magnet pointing towards the Earth’s geographic North is its North pole. (iii) She is using the directive property of magnets, which states that a freely suspended magnet aligns with the Earth’s magnetic field.

items.stem: A shopkeeper keeps a device near the exit that beeps if someone tries to take an item with a special magnetic tag without paying. The tag is deactivated by the cashier upon payment. (i) What property of magnets is likely being used by the deactivation device at the cashier? (ii) Why would a simple piece of iron not work as this special security tag? (iii) What might happen if a customer brings a strong personal magnet near an active tag before reaching the cashier? (Evaluating)
items.answer: (i) The deactivation device likely uses a strong magnetic field or specific magnetic pulses to alter or demagnetize the special tag. (ii) A simple piece of iron would be attracted to any magnet and wouldn’t have a specific state that can be deactivated to prevent the alarm. (iii) A strong personal magnet might interfere with the tag, potentially damaging it, deactivating it unintentionally, or even triggering the alarm prematurely depending on the system’s design.
